prompt: What does every many-to-one join assume about the key on the 'one' side?

choices.text: That the key column is the first column
choices.why: Position plays no part in a join.

choices.text: That each value names exactly one row
choices.why: Right, and a file can claim it without it being true.

choices.text: That both files were exported on the same day
choices.why: That matters for orphans, not for uniqueness.

choices.text: Duplicates are only visible after a join

prompt: What does `validate='many_to_many'` check?

prompt: How does a database hold the 'one' side of a join unique for good?

choices.text: A `DISTINCT` in every query that joins it
choices.why: That hides repeats; it does not prevent them.

choices.text: A primary key or unique constraint
choices.why: Right: a second row with the key is refused.

choices.text: An index on the column, of any kind
choices.why: A plain index allows repeats.

choices.text: A `GROUP BY` on the column in a view
choices.why: A view checks nothing at insert time.

choices.text: The extra rows have blank prices

choices.text: Nothing fails and every row looks real

prompt: In a many-to-one left join, what should happen to the row count?
hint: Each left row meets at most one right row.

choices.text: It grows by the number of matches
choices.why: Matches do not add rows in a many-to-one join.

choices.text: It shrinks by the unmatched rows
choices.why: That is an inner join.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Right; growth means a repeated key on the right.

choices.text: It depends on the size of the right table
choices.why: Size does not matter; uniqueness does.

prompt: Order the diagnosis of a join whose row count changed.
items: Count the rows before the join
Count the rows after the join
If it grew, test the right side's key for repeats
Fix the key, then run the join again
trap: Fixing before counting means fixing a problem you have not measured.
